newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore looks to draw more visitors in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Singapore looks to draw more visitors in 1997.

text.p: Singapore's tourist arrivals rose only slightly in 1996 as attention on Hong Kong's handover lured visitors there, but new efforts to enhance attractions should mean an improvement this year, tourism officials said.
The Singapore Tourist Promotion Board (STPB) on Tuesday said visitor arrivals rose by 2.2 percent in 1996 to 7.3 million, and projected growth of two to five percent for 1997.
Japanese and Taiwanese tourists arrivals to Singapore eased by 0.6 and 6.2 percent respectively, partly due to Hong Kong's prominence ahead of its July 1 handover to China.

"The reason for the decline was primarily due to the switch by our visitors from other destinations to participate in the 1997 countdown," Tan Chin Nam, chief executive of the STPB said, adding that Hong Kong did extremely well in 1996.
While Hong Kong is expected to lure tourists again, it is somewhat constrained by how many visitors it can accommodate.
Japan remains Singapore's top source for visitors. A few months where the rate of decline was as high as five to six percent, however, prompted more aggressive marketing.
Efforts are now being directed to improving Singapore's attractiveness for Japanese tourists and stem the tide to Hong Kong from Singapore and the region.
Singapore has joined with Indonesia to pitch itself as a hub to nearby beach resorts and cultural destinations.
Tourist arrivals began to slump in May but signs of revival became evident during the latter part of the year, Tan said.
In December, nine of 12 major markets registered an increase in visitors to Singapore over the same period last year.
Regional visitors continued to be a mainstay.
Buoyant growth was seen from Malaysia, up 22.8 percent, Indonesia, up 12.3 percent, and Thailand, up 13.4 percent.
The strong Singapore currency and regional competition for the tourist dollar affected the flow of tourists here, but Tan outlined several initiatives to keep Singapore competitive.
"New Asia-Singapore will continue to be our global branding, guiding the reformulation, the packaging of various products ...our existing events will be enhanced," he said.
He cited the Singapore Food Festival, which will be enlarged to become a world gourmet summit, and theme developments in areas such as Chinatown and along the Singapore River.
"If we want to achieve our stretch targets of becoming a tourism capital, we must deal with the basics...how to make the attactiveness of Singapore more solid," Tan added.
The refurbishment of a pre-war convent in the heart of town and the conversion of an adjacent school into an art museum and gallery were recent examples of repackaging existing products.
He said efforts to boost tourism had also taken several new turns, which included the participation of shopowners.
Referring to repackaging as a means of moving performance to another level, he noted: "It cannot be a situation of more of the same. People will get tired of the product."
Tourism 21, overseen by a group of 250 industry members, was also launched recently to offer new directions in tourism and to maximise these contributions to the economy.
Separately, the average hotel occupancy rate fell 1.9 percent to 82.2 percent for 1996. This was attributed to the rise in hotel rooms to 29,500 from about 27,300 last year.
-- Singapore newsroom (65 870 3088)
